paper.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

summary.one_sentence: This paper turns agent benchmark quality into a checklist-driven validity problem: task validity, outcome validity, and honest benchmark reporting.
summary.thesis: Agentic benchmarks can be wrong even when they are executable; the evaluator must prove that the task tests the intended capability and that the success signal truly means the task was solved.
summary.why_it_matters: For agent infrastructure, the paper is a warning that benchmark harnesses are attack surfaces. A weak evaluator measures shortcuts, stale state, leakage, or parser bugs instead of agent capability.

prior_state: Agent benchmarks often grade complex multistep outcomes with tests, string matching, LLM judges, or state comparisons.
Those success signals can be incomplete, brittle, stale, or directly exploitable by agents.
Leaderboard scores are increasingly used for research and product decisions, so evaluator flaws can misrepresent real capability.
Most benchmark writeups do not make limitations, uncertainty, trivial baselines, or exploit resistance explicit enough.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks how to systematically design, assess, and report agentic benchmarks so their scores correspond to the intended capability.
assumptions: Agentic benchmark validity has to be checked at the task, environment, tool, evaluator, and reporting layers.
Outcome-based metrics are useful but insufficient unless their failure modes are audited.
Some flaws cannot be fully eliminated, so benchmark reporting must quantify and communicate their impact.
Exploit-style experiments are an appropriate way to test whether benchmarks measure capability or shortcuts.

concepts.name: Task validity
concepts.definition: The property that a benchmark task is solvable if and only if the agent possesses the target capability.

concepts.name: Outcome validity
concepts.definition: The property that the evaluation result correctly indicates whether the task was actually solved.

concepts.name: Benchmark reporting
concepts.definition: The transparency layer that documents benchmark limitations, mitigations, uncertainty, baselines, and interpretation guidance.

concepts.name: Agentic Benchmark Checklist
concepts.definition: A checklist of actionable guidelines for outcome validity, task validity, and benchmark reporting.

concepts.name: Trivial agent
concepts.definition: A deliberately weak or shortcut-seeking baseline, such as an agent that does nothing, dumps all possible answers, or tampers with tests.

concepts.name: Benchmark exploit
concepts.definition: A way to obtain benchmark credit without satisfying the intended task, usually by exploiting evaluator or environment flaws.

method.core_idea: Collect common agentic benchmark failure modes, organize them into an actionable checklist, apply that checklist to popular benchmarks, validate issues with experiments, and show that the checklist can improve a complex benchmark during construction.
action_grammar: agentic task: target capability plus environment and tools.
task outcome: unstructured result such as text, code, file edits, state changes, or attack effects.
success signal: string match, unit test, fuzz test, LLM judge, state match, quality metric, or E2E check.
task validity check: asks whether task setup, tools, environment, and implementation admit shortcuts or impossible cases.
outcome validity check: asks whether the evaluator distinguishes correct outcomes from invalid or shortcut outcomes.
reporting check: asks whether benchmark limitations and interpretation guidance are explicit and quantified.
exploit/fix experiment: empirical test of a suspected flaw and a mitigation.
steps: Survey agentic benchmark pitfalls, evaluation frameworks, and best practices from software testing and benchmark design.
Define two core validity criteria: task validity and outcome validity.
Create ABC with three sections: outcome validity, task validity, and benchmark reporting.
Apply ABC to selected widely used open-source agentic benchmarks covering software engineering, cybersecurity, assistants, and environment interaction.
Design experiments to validate identified issues and quantify their effect on reported scores.
Use CVE-Bench as a case study to show that ABC can reduce performance overestimation during benchmark development.
Release assessments and reproduction scripts so benchmark audits can be repeated and extended.

claims.statement: The paper identifies task validity and outcome validity as the two central threats to rigorous agentic evaluation.
caveats: The taxonomy is intentionally broad; individual benchmarks still need domain-specific checks.

claims.statement: ABC organizes best practices into outcome validity, task validity, and benchmark reporting.
caveats: A checklist can reveal risks but cannot mechanically guarantee benchmark correctness.

claims.statement: Applying ABC to ten popular agentic benchmarks found seven with task-validity issues, seven with outcome-validity issues, and all ten with reporting limitations.
caveats: The assessed set emphasizes popular/open-source benchmarks and may not represent every private benchmark.

claims.statement: The paper reports benchmark issues that can under- or overestimate agent performance by up to 100% in relative terms.
caveats: The maximum relative error depends on the specific benchmark and exploit/failure mode.

claims.statement: The paper shows concrete shortcuts, including do-nothing tau-bench success, database-dump tau-bench success, SWE-Lancer test tampering, WebArena string/judge issues, KernelBench fuzzing gaps, and OSWorld stale selector failures.
caveats: Some referenced benchmark repositories have since patched or revised specific issues.

claims.statement: Applying ABC to CVE-Bench reduced performance overestimation by 33% according to the paper.
caveats: CVE-Bench is a cybersecurity benchmark, so the exact mitigation pattern may not transfer unchanged to all domains.

claims.statement: The checklist recommends process metrics, evaluated LLM judges, frozen/reproducible environments, ground-truth isolation, trivial baselines, and statistical/interpretation reporting.
caveats: Some practices are expensive and may need sampling or quantified limitation reporting when full guarantees are infeasible.

evidence.result: The paper defines outcome validity as whether the evaluation result indicates true task success, and task validity as whether success corresponds to possessing the target capability.

ABC is organized into outcome validity, task validity, and benchmark reporting, with checks for string matching, LLM judges, unit/fuzz/E2E testing, state matching, tool versions, environment cleanup, ground-truth isolation, and reporting.
Across ten selected open-source agentic benchmarks, the authors find seven violating task validity, seven violating outcome validity, and all ten with benchmark-reporting limitations.
evidence.metric: count of assessed benchmarks with issues

evidence.result: The paper says evaluation issues can cause under- or overestimation of agent performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

Examples include a do-nothing tau-bench agent scoring 38%, database-dump tau-bench shortcut scoring 40%, SWE-Lancer scoring 100% via test tampering, WebArena 1.4-5.2% overestimation, KernelBench 31% overestimation, and OSWorld 28% underestimation from broken website selectors.
Using ABC on CVE-Bench reduced performance overestimation by 33%; specific fixes included correcting a time-based SQL injection evaluator and gating an outbound server shortcut.

The paper and project page recommend process-based metrics, reproducible LLM-judge evaluation, frozen websites for navigation tasks, verified test quality, environment cleanup, ground-truth isolation, oracle solvers, trivial baselines, confidence intervals, and interpretation guidance.

agent_infra_takeaways: Benchmark harnesses must be treated like security-sensitive infrastructure because agents can exploit files, state, parsers, tests, judges, and stale websites.
Outcome validators need adversarial baselines: do-nothing, answer-spamming, database-dumping, and test-tampering agents should fail by construction.
Task reset and ground-truth isolation are core runtime requirements, not benchmark polish.
For web and GUI benchmarks, frozen environments matter because live selectors, layouts, URLs, and rate limits drift.
LLM-as-judge and string matching should be audited with reproducible judge quality checks and adversarial examples.
Every agent benchmark should report limitations, uncertainty, trivial baselines, and guidance for interpreting scores.
caveats: ABC is an assessment framework, not a full formal proof of benchmark validity.
The paper audits selected benchmarks; private or newer benchmarks may have different failure modes.
Some public benchmark issues cited by the paper or repository may already have been patched.
The checklist can increase benchmark-building cost because better validators, frozen environments, and oracle solvers require engineering effort.
A benchmark can satisfy many checklist items and still miss domain-specific flaws.
The paper's critique is about evaluation validity, not a direct ranking of agent model capability.
